pages.text:
How a case file works

Every case in this book is a real event from Australian history. Something happened. People
who were there told different stories. Some people were never asked at all. Your job is to read
the file, ask careful questions, and write a finding. There is no answer at the back. Eureka
Stockade, 1854 — Who fired first? — is the worked example. Every other case is built the same
way.

Part

1. The opener
2. Read
3. Ask

4. Decide
5. Super Sleuths
(optional)

What you do

A short story, written to look authentic. In the Eureka case this is Nell’s
Diary, a child’s notebook that stops at the first shot. What’s true — who
is made up, who is real, and what isn’t certain — sits only in the teacher
notes, not on the story pages themselves.
Read the opener through to the moment in dispute.
A short account of what is agreed, then three real witnesses on one page.
Each has a period portrait, or a plain silhouette if none exists, a short
summary of what they said, the source, and the same three questions:
What did they say they saw? Could they really have seen it? Why might
they say it?
Write one finding in a My finding box. In the Eureka case: Who fired
first? Rebels, soldiers, or we can’t know — and why.
For students who want to dig deeper: the full witness files under seven
headings, a source pack, a timeline, evidence for and against, what we
still can’t know, and a sure / maybe / guess check. This page is reached
by a hyperlink, not a QR code.

RULES FOR EVERY CASE
Real sources only. Words in quotation marks come from a named record. Do not invent what the
sources do not say.

Never invent likenesses. Do not generate or invent a likeness of a real person. Use a real period
portrait that is free to reuse, or a plain silhouette with a name card.

Flag conflicts. Where the records disagree, say that they disagree. Leave open what the record
leaves open. Do not resolve a dispute the sources do not settle.

Teacher notes. What’s true — who is made up, who is real, what isn’t certain, the care the case

needs, and the source and rights of each picture — sits only in the teacher notes, not on the opener’s
student pages.

Contents

One book, Years 4 to 10, in chronological order of the event. All 13 cases in this sample are written in
full. A short by-year-level index follows the main list, so a teacher can still find a year at a glance.
Protection comes after Cook (1770) and before Eliza Fraser (1836), by the date of the 1787
instructions that open the typographic page and frame the question. The file’s sharp focus is later —
the Aborigines Act 1905 (WA), the 1928 deputation, and A. O. Neville’s 1937 conference — but the
case is written as a long question that starts with that founding promise. Placing it at 1905 would put
it after Federation and hide the frame the opener is built around.
Lambing Flat is placed by the first major riot at Burrangong on 12 December 1860 (the file covers
the 1860–61 sequence, including 30 June and 14 July 1861). Burke and Wills is placed by the deaths
at Cooper Creek in late June 1861, which is the question that file asks. The cameleers follow those
two 1860–61 crises, as a longer arc from the 1860s through the Immigration Restriction Act 1901.
The hospital ship Centaur is placed by the sinking on 14 May 1943, after Broken Hill (1 January
1915) and before the Freedom Ride (February 1965). Mabo is placed by the High Court decision of 3
June 1992; the writ was filed in May 1982.
The written cases follow the pattern on the previous page: an opener, three short witnesses, a
finding, and an optional Super Sleuths page. The Batavia case starts with the escape-room story In
Case of Emergency, then opens with a typographic page from the night the Batavia struck the reef.
Eureka Stockade opens with Nell’s Diary. Several files are drafts, pending consultation: Cook at
Kamay with Gweagal and Dharawal communities of Kamay; Protection with relevant Aboriginal
communities in Western Australia, including Noongar communities and those connected with
Moore River; Eliza Fraser with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation; the cameleers wherever it
touches First Nations histories, including the Canning Stock Route; Federation as a draft pending
consultation; the Freedom Ride with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially Moree
and Walgett; and Mabo with the Meriam people of Mer; all with AIATSIS guidance where First
Nations histories are taught.

THE UNFINISHED VOYAGE · YEAR 4 · READ

What can the records still not tell us?
The Unfinished Voyage, 1629

This file is about a shipwreck, and about the records that remain. People died when the ship struck, and
many more were killed later, before help came. This file does not describe those deaths. A note for
teachers is at the end of the case.

Read the page from the night the ship struck. Then read what this file can agree on. After that, three
witnesses will be asked the same three questions.

CASE FILE: BATAVIA / 1629
Date of incident
Location

4 June 1629 (wreck found 1963; journal survives in the Dutch archives)

Houtman Abrolhos, off the coast of what is now Western Australia

Status
The wreck and the mutiny are not in doubt · The records are still
unfinished
Key claims still disputed

– What can the records still not tell us?
– Which gaps were never written, and which papers were lost later?
– Why do later tellings disagree about the numbers?

WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1629 RECORDS, AND AFTER
The Batavia was a ship of the Dutch East India Company, the VOC. It left the island of Texel, in the
Netherlands, in late October 1628, bound for the city then also called Batavia, now Jakarta. Sources do not
all agree on the exact day it left, or on the exact number of people on board at the start. Many lists say
about 322 people were on the ship when it struck the reef.
In the early hours of 4 June 1629 the ship struck a reef in the Houtman Abrolhos, off the coast of what is
now Western Australia. The journal of the commandeur, Francisco Pelsaert, opens on that Monday
morning. About 40 people drowned at the wreck. The rest reached low islands nearby. Some later
retellings give a much higher number for those first deaths. This file keeps the number recorded from the
Dutch papers: about 40.
Pelsaert, the skipper Ariaen Jacobsz, and others left in the ship’s longboat to look for water, and then to
find help. They reached the city of Batavia after a long voyage. Pelsaert came back in a ship called the
Sardam, in mid-September 1629.
While they were away, a mutiny was led by the under-merchant Jeronimus Cornelisz. Many people were
killed before the rescue. A group of soldiers, led by Wiebbe Hayes, found water on a higher island and held
out. Hayes reached the rescue ship first.
Pelsaert wrote a long journal. The handwritten journal still survives in the Dutch National Archives. Other
papers from the ship, including the lists of the crew’s pay, have been lost. The wreck was found in 1963.
Timbers and objects from the ship are now in the Western Australian Museum.
No one who was there wrote a full day-by-day record of the weeks of the mutiny as they happened.

Three witnesses

The same three questions for each: What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? ·
Why might they say it? Two have a plain silhouette, not a photograph. The third is a ship silhouette,
for the wreck itself. No likeness of a real person has been invented. No contemporary portraits of
Pelsaert or Hayes are known for this file.

A NOTE ON THIS FILE
This file is about a shipwreck, and about the records that remain. People died when the ship struck,
and many more were killed later, before help came. This file does not describe those deaths. A note
for teachers is at the end of the case.

Francisco Pelsaert

Commandeur of the Batavia · Wrote the journal · Died 1630

The main written record of the wreck, the rescue, and the questions asked afterwards.
Source. Pelsaert’s journal, held in the Nationaal Archief, The Hague, VOC 1.04.02, inv. nr. 1098, folios 232–
317. A silhouette is used. No contemporary portrait of Pelsaert is known for this file.

What they said. His journal opens on the morning the ship struck, 4 June 1629. He
A silhouette, not a likeness.

records the wreck, the landing on the islands, the longboat voyage for help, and his return
on the Sardam. He also wrote down what people told him later about the weeks he had
missed, and the decisions of the ship’s council after the rescue.

Could they really have seen it? He was there for the wreck, and for the rescue. He was not

on the islands during the weeks of the mutiny. For those days he had to rely on what other
people later said. A commandeur writing for the VOC also had to explain himself to his masters.

Why might they say it? To record the loss of the ship, to account for the cargo, and to set
down what he had learned about the mutiny. A journal written for the company is still one
person’s record. It is the best written source we have. It is not the only kind of evidence.

Wiebbe Hayes

A soldier on the Batavia · Led the group that held the higher island

The man who found water, kept his group together, and reached the rescue ship first.
Source. Hayes is known mainly through Pelsaert’s journal, which records what he had done and how he
was later promoted. No book of Hayes’s own is known to survive. The journal sometimes spells his name
Haijes. A silhouette is used. No contemporary portrait is known for this file.

What they said. We do not have a long statement in Hayes’s own hand. Pelsaert wrote
A silhouette, not a likeness.

that Hayes and his soldiers had found water and food on a higher island, that they had held
out against the mutineers, and that they had captured Cornelisz. When the Sardam came,
Hayes reached Pelsaert first. Pelsaert later made him a sergeant.

Could they really have seen it? Hayes was there for the weeks Pelsaert missed. He could see
what happened on his own island, and in the fights with the mutineers. He could not see
everything that happened on the other islands. What we read is mostly Pelsaert’s record of
Hayes, not Hayes’s own page.

Why might they say it? If the journal is right, Hayes wanted the rescue ship to hear his

group’s story first. After the rescue he was rewarded. We still have to remember that his voice
comes to us through someone else’s journal.

What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________

The wreck of the Batavia

The ship itself, found in 1963 · Objects now in the Western Australian Museum

Silent evidence: timbers, a stone portico, coins, and other objects raised from the reef.
Source. The wreck was found on Morning Reef in 1963. From 1970, teams from the Western Australian
Museum raised part of the stern and many objects. They can be seen in the Shipwrecks Museum in
Fremantle. This card is the wreck, not a person. No living archaeologist is pictured.

What they said. The objects do not speak in words. They show that the ship was real, that
A ship silhouette, not a
picture of the wreck itself.

it carried building stone and silver, and that it broke on that reef. They cannot, by
themselves, tell us what was said on the islands, or fill in a day that no one wrote down.

Could they really have seen it? The wreck has sat on the reef since 1629. It can show us the
ship. It cannot see the people on the islands. What we learn from it depends on how carefully it
was raised, and on how we read it beside the journal, not instead of the journal.

Why might they say it? A wreck is not trying to persuade us. That is a strength. It is also a
limit. Objects prove some things very well, and other things not at all.

Why it still matters

The Batavia is often told as a thriller, or as a horror story. The file is still open because some
papers from the ship were lost, because the commandeur was not there for the worst weeks,
and because later tellings do not always agree. Learning to see what a record can prove, and
what it cannot, is the work of this book.

Super Sleuths

Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. Some
harder parts of this story are kept in the Teacher Note, not here.

Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/batavia-case/#sleuth

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. The night the ship struck
Pelsaert’s journal opens on Monday morning, 4 June 1629, the second day of Whitsuntide, with a
bright, clear, full moon, on the reef of Frederick Houtman. The Western Australian Museum’s
account of that night says a white gleam of breaking surf was seen, and that the skipper, Ariaen
Jacobsz, as head of the watch, took it for moonlight.
The opening page of this case uses those documented facts, set in type. It is not a photograph of the
journal, and it is not a whole translation of the entry.
Question. What can a short opening, written after the shock of the wreck, actually prove — and what
can it not?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. Why the numbers do not match
Careful museum work often gives about 322 people on board when the ship struck, and about 40 who
drowned at the wreck. A Western Australian Museum history page also says the ship left Texel on 29
October 1628 with 341 people. Other pages and books give 27 or 28 October, or “about 330.” The
National Museum of Australia has said that about 100 people died in the immediate aftermath of the
collision. That does not match the Dutch papers’ figure of about 40.
Question. When two museums disagree, what should a case file do instead of picking the more
dramatic number?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. The weeks no commandeur was there to write down
Pelsaert left in the longboat and came back in mid-September. The worst weeks on the islands
happened while he was away. His journal of those weeks is not a diary he kept on the spot. It is what
he later wrote from questions, confessions, and other people’s memories.
Question. How should we read a record of days the writer did not see?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER

4. Papers that really were lost
Pelsaert’s handwritten journal still survives in the Dutch National Archives (VOC 1098, folios 232–
317). It is not right to say, as a fact, that “pages we know once existed” are missing from that journal,
or that “statements stop mid-sentence,” unless a better source shows that. What has been lost,
according to later museum research, includes the ship’s muster rolls and pay registers, which would
have named the crew.
Question. What is the difference between a page that was never written, and a list that was written
and later lost?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. What the museum objects can prove
The wreck was found in 1963. In the 1970s the Western Australian Museum raised part of the stern, a
carved stone portico, and many smaller objects. They prove the ship, and something of what it
carried. They cannot, alone, tell us what was said on the islands.
Question. If you could place one object beside one page of the journal, which two would you choose,
and why?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Other Dutch marks on this coast
The Batavia was not the first Dutch ship on this coast. In 1616 Dirk Hartog left a pewter plate at Cape
Inscription, on what is now Dirk Hartog Island. The plate’s short inscription is complete; it is not an
unfinished fragment. In late 1696 Willem de Vlamingh landed on the island he named ’t Eylandt ’t
Rottenest (Rottnest) and, in 1697, replaced Hartog’s plate with a new one, taking the old plate home.
Each voyage left a different kind of trace: a plate, a journal, a wreck and its objects. That is a better
comparison than a claim that all the Dutch papers have the same “blank stretches.”
Question. What can a plate prove that a journal cannot — and the other way round?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Two men left on the mainland
In mid-November 1629, after the trials on the islands, Pelsaert’s council left two men, Wouter Loos
and Jan Pelgrom de Bye, on the Australian mainland. Their fate is unknown. Later stories about their
lives there, including stories of contact with Aboriginal people of the mid-west coast, have not been
proved. This file does not invent an ending for them.

8. A book from 1647, and a journal from 1629
In 1647 a Dutch book, Ongeluckige Voyagie, van’t schip Batavia, was printed from Pelsaert’s journal.
It was popular, and it was reprinted. A printed book is not the same thing as the handwritten journal
in the archives. The 1647 engravings are old and useful, but they are pictures made in Europe, years
later. Some of them are too hard for this year level.
Question. Why might a famous later book still be the wrong proof for a question about the original
journal?

Teacher Note

THE UNFINISHED VOYAGE · YEAR 4 · TEACHER NOTE
This file is about a shipwreck, and about the records that remain. People died when the ship
struck, and many more were killed later, before help came. This file does not describe those
deaths. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.

Where this case sits, and why

The user’s draft was a Year 4 school-camp investigation, “Batavia Cold Case / The Unfinished
Voyage.” It comes first in this chronological book, Year 4, because the wreck is dated 4 June 1629. In
a teaching sequence it belongs with Year 4, as an earlier European voyage on the Western Australian
coast. The Start here escape-room page remains at the front of this case.
The book starts at Year 4. Year 3 knowledge descriptions (AC9HS3K01, local community change;
AC9HS3K02, national days, symbols and emblems) do not fit a 1629 VOC voyage. Year 3/4 learners
can still read this file; the honest knowledge code is Year 4. AC9HS4K02 is “the causes of the
establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788.” That is not, on its face, a Batavia code.
The official elaborations, though, ask students to examine earlier voyages along the route to
Australia and along the Australian coastline (the examples include Dirk Hartog, Willem Jansz, Abel
Tasman, and James Cook) in order to understand how knowledge of those routes later made a
colony thinkable. The Batavia is a VOC trader, not one of the named explorers in the elaboration.
This file uses AC9HS4K02 by that official path, and says so here. It does not pretend the v9
descriptor is still the old v8 wording about “world navigators, explorers or traders” (ACHASSK084).
The inquiry heart of the case — what sources can and cannot tell us — is also a Year 4 skills matter
(AC9HS4S03, AC9HS4S04). Those skills codes may be mentioned to teachers; they are not claimed
as the History knowledge code on the student pages.

The escape room first

Give students the escape-room story In Case of Emergency first, so they walk the true voyage in
order as background, before they attempt this case. The teacher card How to run it (at the back of

the picture book, and in the app menu) has hooks, grouping, and a debrief. Then open this case file.
The companion app is at https://robmac10.github.io/batavia-escape-room/ ; the QR on the Start
here page uses a small folded story-map emblem, with a you-are-here mark.

The opening page

The opening page is a typographic setting, not a photograph of Pelsaert’s journal, and not a
facsimile. That explanation is kept off the student page so the night can be read as a scene. The date,
the reef of Frederick Houtman, Whitsuntide, and the bright, clear, full moon follow the opening of
Pelsaert’s journal (Nationaal Archief, VOC 1098). The white gleam of surf, and the skipper taking it
for moonlight, follow the Western Australian Museum’s account of that night (Jacobsz as head of
the watch). The English wording is a short rendering for this file, not a long extract copied from a

Care, and what was not used from the draft

The fuller record of the Batavia includes the murder of many people, including children, sexual

violence, torture used in the later examinations, and executions. None of that is described on the
student pages. A short content note sits at the front of the case. Preview any extra source, including
Mike Dash, Batavia’s Graveyard, and the 1647 engravings, before you share it. Some of those
pictures are too hard for Year 3/4.

The user’s draft was framed as a class file after a school camp, with “museum notes,” “journal
copies,” and “ferry diary pages.” This file is written as a historical case for any classroom, not as a

named camp report, and it does not invent a ferry diary as a 1629 source. The draft said that days in
the records stay short or empty, that numbers do not match, that some statements stop mid-

sentence, and that “pages we know once existed are still missing.” The disagreement about numbers
is real, and is used. The fact that Pelsaert was absent for the mutiny weeks, so those days were not
written as a spot diary, is real, and is used. A general claim that journal pages known to have existed
are missing, or that statements stop mid-sentence, was not established for this file. The manuscript
of the journal survives at folios 232–317. What later research does record as lost includes the ship’s
muster rolls and pay registers (Western Australian Museum, “Databases of the people aboard the
VOC ships”). Those lost lists are the honest example. The draft also compared “unfinished sections”
in the 1616 Hartog plate and in de Vlamingh’s 1696 notes. Hartog’s pewter inscription is short and
complete; de Vlamingh copied it and replaced it in 1697. This file does not invent blank stretches in
those records. Super Sleuths 6 asks a fairer question: what different kinds of trace each Dutch
voyage left.

Facts checked, and flags

Wreck: early hours of 4 June 1629, Morning Reef, Houtman Abrolhos, Wallabi Group. Journal
opening: Monday morning, second day of Whitsuntide, bright clear full moon, reef of Frederick
Houtman. About 40 drowned at the wreck, from the Dutch papers and the Western Australian
Museum’s wreck entry. The National Museum of Australia’s “about 100 people died in the
immediate aftermath” is treated as a conflict, not as the agreed figure. Departure: late October 1628
from Texel. Sources give 27, 28 or 29 October; a 2022 Western Australian Museum history page
gives 29 October and 341 people at departure. About 322 is the figure often given for those on board
at the wreck. The student page uses careful wording and does not silently pick one date. Rescue:
longboat voyage to the city of Batavia; Pelsaert returned on the Sardam in mid-September 1629.
Hayes reached him first and was later promoted to sergeant. Cornelisz led the mutiny; he and others
were tried by the ship’s council. Two men, Wouter Loos and Jan Pelgrom de Bye, were left on the
mainland in mid-November 1629; their fate is unknown. Pelsaert died in September 1630. All of the
1629 people named here are long deceased, so dates may be given. Living archaeologists and
museum staff, if named in class, get no dates and no photographs. No photos of human remains are
used.

This is not, in the main, a First Nations case, and the envelope is not stamped “Draft, pending

consultation.” The islands and the nearby mainland, though, are part of a coast cared for by
Aboriginal people long before 1629. The two marooned men, and later unproved stories of contact,

are the place where that care is needed. If a class takes Super Sleuths 7 further, it should do so with
the relevant Aboriginal communities of the mid-west coast, and with AIATSIS guidance. This file
does not invent an ending, and it does not name a language group unless a teacher is working with
that community.

No verified contemporary portraits of Pelsaert, Hayes, or Lucretia Jans (also van der Mijlen) were
found for this file. Later paintings sometimes used as “portraits” of them are not their likenesses and
are not used. The witness images are plain silhouettes, or a ship symbol for the wreck.

Curriculum and classroom

Year 4, written so Year 3/4 learners and interested general readers can both stay with it. The useful
work is to sit with an unfinished record without inventing a missing page, and without turning the

case into a horror story. The finding options include “we can’t know.” Lucretia Jans is not a witness
card here: the sources about her include material that is not for this year level. Teachers who
introduce her should preview first, and should not invent a portrait.

Resources

Students can also read the page from the night of the wreck as an interactive book, on a
tablet or phone. The page on screen is the same story as the pages in this book. Use it in
class, or send the link home. The app is built and ready; it should be published only when
you say go. The QR code uses a ship emblem at the centre.

Kamay / Botany Bay
Excursion day. The photocopy is from 1768.

The sign says Kamay / Botany Bay. The water is ordinary. That’s what gets me.
In the photocopy his instructions say, with the Consent of the Natives. They even
capitalised Consent.
I walked down to the sand where the landing is supposed to have happened and
tried to imagine two men on the rock, and a boat that doesn’t turn around.
He wrote that they seemed resolved to oppose our landing. That’s in his journal.
He still landed.
I kept waiting for the bit where somebody says yes. It isn’t in the pack.

The quiet is worse once you know the orders had that word in them.
— on the bus back

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
Draft, pending consultation with Gweagal and Dharawal communities of Kamay, including families
at La Perouse, and with AIATSIS guidance. This case describes a landing in which muskets were fired
and a man was struck by small shot. The two Gweagal men who opposed the landing are not named
in the 1770 journals. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.

COOK AT KAMAY, 1770 · YEAR 9 · READ

Cook at Kamay, 1770

Did he have the consent of the natives?

What is agreed

Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

On 30 July 1768 the Admiralty issued additional (“secret”) instructions to Lieutenant James
Cook. They told him: “You are also with the Consent of the Natives to take Possession of
Convenient Situations in the Country in the Name of the King of Great Britain: Or: if you find
the Country uninhabited take Possession for his Majesty by setting up Proper Marks and
Inscriptions, as first discoverers and possessors.”

The Endeavour entered Kamay (Botany Bay) in late April 1770. Cook’s journal dates the landing
Sunday, 29 April. Joseph Banks records the same landing under 28 April. Historians treat these
as the same event; the dating difference is flagged, not hidden.

Cook, Banks, Dr Solander and the Ra‘iatean navigator Tupaia (written “Tupia” in the journals)
went in toward the south shore. Most people moved away. Two men came down and opposed
the landing. After an exchange that included musket fire, a stone thrown, small shot that struck
one man, and darts or lances thrown at the visitors, the two men went off. The landing party
went to the houses, left beads and other things, and took away spears (Banks: forty or fifty
lances).

The journals do not record a grant of consent. The next day Cook wrote that presents could not
entice people to the officer on shore: “all they seem’d to want was for us to be gone.”

Three witnesses

COOK AT KAMAY, 1770 · YEAR 9 · ASK
Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness.
Ask the same three questions of each.

James Cook

Lieutenant, commander of HMB Endeavour · journal, 29–30 April 1770

His own journal of the landing, and of the next day.

What they said

James Cook, portrait after
Nathaniel Dance, late
eighteenth century. Public
domain. Not a picture of the
landing at Kamay.

On 29 April he wrote that, as the boats approached, “they all made off,
except 2 Men, who seem’d resolved to oppose our landing.” He could not
understand their words, “for neither us nor Tupia could understand one
word they said.” After muskets were fired, including small shot that struck
one man, he wrote that the two men went off. The next day he recorded that
presents could not bring people to the officer on shore: “all they seem’d to
want was for us to be gone.”

Could they have seen it?

He was in the boats and on the shore. He was also the officer who ordered
the shots, and the man writing the official journal. He could not understand
the language. He first thought a gesture was an invitation, then wrote that
he had been mistaken.

Why might they say it?

To record a landing for the Admiralty, and to explain the use of muskets. A
commander’s journal is evidence of what he said happened. It is not a
neutral film of the beach, and it is not the Gweagal men’s account.
Source. Cook’s journal, Sunday 29 April and 30 April 1770. A widely used transcription is
quoted by the State Library of NSW (“Violence on the shore”; “Eight days in Kamay”) from
Safe 1/71. Wording here follows that published journal text.

pages.text:
Joseph Banks

Naturalist on the Endeavour · journal, 28 April 1770 (his dating of the landing)

A second journal of the same afternoon, written by a man in the boats who
was not in command.

What they said
Joseph Banks, eighteenthcentury portrait. Public
domain. Not a picture from
Kamay.

Banks wrote that as the boats approached the rocks, “two of the men came
down upon them, each armd with a lance of about 10 feet long.” “They calld
to us very loud in a harsh sounding Language of which neither us or Tupia
understood a word, shaking their lances and menacing, in all appearance
resolvd to dispute our landing to the utmost tho they were but two and we
30 or 40 at least.” He recorded them “waving to us to be gone.” After small
shot struck the elder man on the legs, he “ran up to the house… and soon
returnd with a sheild.” Lances were thrown; more small shot was fired; the
two men ran away. Banks then wrote: “We however thought it no improper
measure to take away with us all the lances which we could find about the
houses, amounting in number to forty or fifty.”

Could they have seen it?

He was there, close enough to describe paint, weapons, and distances. He
also wanted plants, and he helped to justify taking the spears. A private
scientific journal is still one man’s account.

Why might they say it?

To keep a private scientific journal of what he saw, including the taking of
the spears — which he felt the need to justify as “no improper measure.”
That phrase is evidence of a choice, not of permission.
Source. The Endeavour Journal of Sir Joseph Banks, entry beginning “1770 April 28.”
Wikisource transcription; the original is held by the State Library of NSW (Banks Papers,
Series 03.02).

pages.text:
The Gweagal men at Kamay

Two men who opposed the landing · not named in the 1770 journals

This card does not invent a speech. It sets out what the visiting journals
said the two men did, and one phrase a shipboard artist later published as
their call.

What they said
Silhouettes, not likenesses.
The 1770 journals do not
name the two men or carry a
portrait of them. A later
identification of one man as
Cooman is recorded, and
disputed, in Super Sleuths.

The journals say the two men came down armed, called out, waved the
boats away, and stood their ground against a much larger landing party.
After musket fire, one man was struck by small shot, fetched a shield, and
lances were thrown. Parkinson later printed the call “Warra warra wai.”
The journals do not record a grant of consent, and they do not record the
two men’s own words in their own language, written down by them.

Could they have seen it?

They were on their own Country, on the rock and the beach, at close range.
The problem is not their presence. The problem is the record: everything on
this card has been filtered through English journals and a 1773 book. We
cannot hear the conversation they had with each other, which Banks said
they seemed to hold “earnestly.”

Why might they say it?

They were opposing a landing on their Country. This file does not invent a
motive beyond what the journals describe, and it does not translate their
call as if the 1770 writers had understood it.
Source. Cook’s journal, 29–30 April 1770, and Banks’s journal, 28 April 1770, as above.
Sydney Parkinson, A Journal of a Voyage to the South Seas (1773), records that the two men
were “often crying to us, Warra warra wai.” Senior Gweagal knowledge holder Dr Shayne
Williams has explained that phrase, in later published comments used by the State Library of
NSW, as meaning “you are all dead” — an observation, in his account, rather than a simple
threat. Some later oral histories name one of the men Cooman; other local voices have said
there is no single agreed identification. This file does not choose a name and then pretend the
journals used it.

Why it still matters

The word “consent” is in the 1768 instructions. The 1770 journals are still the main written
record of the first hours at Kamay. Whether those hours, or the later flag-raising in the Torres
Strait, could count as consent is not only a history-class puzzle. It sits under later arguments
about sovereignty, about Country, and about objects taken from the beach.

COOK AT KAMAY, 1770 · YEAR 9 · SUPER SLEUTHS

Super Sleuths

Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. This
file is a draft, pending consultation with Gweagal and Dharawal communities of Kamay, and with
AIATSIS guidance.

Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/cook-case/#sleuth

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. Two dates for one landing
Cook dates the landing Sunday 29 April 1770. Banks dates the same landing 28 April. Historians
treat these as one event, with a shipboard dating difference.
Question. Why might two men in the same boats write two dates, and what is lost if a later account
silently picks one?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. Naming the two men
The 1770 journals do not name them. Some later oral histories, including accounts linked to Biddy
Giles and to descendant Rodney Kelly, name one man Cooman. Other local voices, including
comments reported from the Gujaga Foundation, have said there is no single agreed identification.
Maria Nugent and Gaye Sculthorpe have written that there is “no consensus” that Cooman was one of
the two.
Question. What changes when a later name is printed as if the journal had used it?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. “Warra warra wai”
Sydney Parkinson, in 1773, printed that the two men were “often crying to us, Warra warra wai.” Dr
Shayne Williams has explained the phrase, in later published comments, as meaning “you are all
dead.” The 1770 journals do not give a translation.
Question. What is the difference between a phrase written down by a visitor, and a meaning
explained later by a knowledge holder?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Possession Island, 22 August 1770
Cook did not take formal possession at Kamay. He later recorded a flag-raising at Possession Island
(Bedanug / Tuidin) in the Torres Strait. That is a different place, and a later date. This case’s question
is still about consent.
Question. If consent was required at convenient situations, what does a later ceremony on a different
island show, and what does it not show?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The spears, and a shield
Banks recorded taking forty or fifty lances from the houses. Some objects from the voyage are still in
collections overseas. A shield in the British Museum has often been linked to this landing; that link is
now disputed. This file does not treat the attribution as settled.
Question. What can a later museum object prove about an afternoon in 1770, and what can it not
prove?

photograph. The photocopied lines are real. The instructions extract is from the Admiralty’s
additional (“secret”) instructions to Lieutenant James Cook, 30 July 1768: “You are also with
the Consent of the Natives to take Possession of Convenient Situations in the Country in the
Name of the King of Great Britain: Or: if you find the Country uninhabited take Possession for
his Majesty by setting up Proper Marks and Inscriptions, as first discoverers and possessors.”

Did “protection” ever mean protection?
The 1787 instructions, the Aborigines Act 1905 (WA), and A. O. Neville

DRAFT, PENDING CONSULTATION

Draft, pending consultation. This file asks whether “protection” ever meant protection, including for
Aboriginal people in Western Australia under the Aborigines Act 1905, and at places such as the
Moore River Native Settlement. Teach it with care, and with AIATSIS guidance. A note for teachers is
at the end of the case.

These words were not spoken in one room.

The typographic page is three dated records, not one speech. The first lines are from the
Crown’s instructions to Arthur Phillip, 25 April 1787. The middle lines are from the Western
Australian Act reserved on 23 December 1905. The last question was asked by A. O. Neville at
Canberra in April 1937. The line “They called it protection.” is this file’s frame. It is not a
quotation from 1787, or from 1905, or from 1937.
Read the typographic page, and this handover. Then read what this file can agree on. After that,
three witnesses will be asked the same three questions.

CASE FILE: PROTECTION / 1787–1937

Date of incident 25 April 1787 · Aborigines Act 1905 (WA), in force 20 April 1906 · deputation 9
March 1928 · Canberra conference 21–23 April 1937
Location
St James’s, London · Western Australia, including Perth and the Moore River Native
Settlement · Canberra

Status
The word was “protection.” · Whether it ever meant protection
is still the question
Key claims still disputed
– Did the 1787 instructions ever amount to protection in practice?
– What did the 1905 Act protect, and whom did it place under a Chief Protector?
– What can Neville’s 1937 words, and the 1928 deputation, still show us?

What is agreed
From the 1787 instructions, the 1905 Act, and the 1928 and 1937 records.

WHAT IS AGREED

“conciliate their affections,” to enjoin subjects to “live in amity and kindness with them,” and to
punish anyone who would “wantonly destroy them.” The same instructions also asked how
intercourse “may be turned to the advantage of this country.”
The Parliament of Western Australia passed “An Act to make provision for the better protection and
care of the Aboriginal inhabitants of Western Australia,” reserved on 23 December 1905, with royal
assent proclaimed on 27 April 1906, and proclaimed to commence on 20 April 1906. Section 4
charged a department with “promoting the welfare of the aborigines” and “generally assisting in the
preservation and well-being of the aborigines.” Section 8, as enacted in 1905, said: “The Chief
Protector shall be the legal guardian of every aboriginal and half-caste child until such child attains
the age of sixteen years.” A 1911 amendment added words about the exclusion of the rights of the
mother of an illegitimate half-caste child. This file does not print the 1911 words as if they had been in
the 1905 Act on the day it was reserved.
Auber Octavius Neville was Chief Protector of Aborigines in Western Australia from 1915 to 1936,
and Commissioner of Native Affairs from 1936 until he retired in 1940. The Moore River Native
Settlement was established in 1918, under the 1905 Act.
On 9 March 1928 William Harris, a Noongar man, led an Aboriginal deputation to Premier Philip
Collier in Perth. They asked for the 1905 Act to be repealed, for equal rights, and for Moore River to
be closed. The Act was not repealed at that meeting.
At Canberra, from 21 to 23 April 1937, a conference of Commonwealth and State Aboriginal
authorities heard Neville, by then Commissioner of Native Affairs, and recorded both his speech and
a resolution on “absorption.” The wording on the typographic page is from that official report.
The words “aboriginal” and “half-caste” in the quoted Act and report are the record’s words, not this
file’s chosen language for people now.

Could they really have seen it? He was Chief Protector, then

Commissioner, and he was in the room in Canberra when the official report
was made. He could speak about the Act he administered, and about the
policy he wanted. He could not speak for the people the Act named, and he
could not see, from that conference table, every life lived under it. His
language is the language of 1937 official policy. This file keeps it, because it is
what he said. It is not this file’s language.

Why might they say it? To argue for a long-range policy of absorption,

and to defend the powers already in the Western Australian Act. A man
called Protector was describing the taking of children as a means to “merge”
and “forget.” Students can ask what the title “Protector” was doing in that
sentence.

from the checked record is the deputation itself. On 9 March 1928 Harris led
Aboriginal men to the Premier of Western Australia. They asked for the 1905

Could they really have seen it? He was there. He had lived under the

Why it still matters

The word “protection” is still used about laws, offices, and children. The people named in the
1905 Act, and the families connected to Moore River and to the 1928 deputation, have not gone
away. Later inquiries, including Bringing Them Home in 1997, asked what those laws did. This
file does not pretend that a Year 10 finding can close that history. It asks students to sit with the
word the Acts used, and with the words of a Protector and of the men who walked in to see the
Premier, and to decide what the record will bear.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. “Savages” and “Natives” in the 1787 manuscript
The typographic page follows the Documenting a Democracy transcription of the 25 April 1787
instructions, and uses the standing word “Natives.” That transcription prints “Savages Natives,”
which usually means the handwritten original had a change. Historical Records of Australia prints
“natives.” This file does not print “Savages” as if it were the chosen word.
Question. Why might a clerk strike one word and write another, and what is lost if a later copy
hides the change?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. The 1911 words that were not in the 1905 Act as reserved
Section 8, as reserved in 1905, made the Chief Protector the legal guardian of every aboriginal and
half-caste child until the age of sixteen. The 1911 amendment (No. 42 of 1911) added “to the exclusion
of the rights of the mother of an illegitimate half-caste child.” Some later printings set those words in
the same section without making the date of the change clear.
Question. What changes when a later clause is silently folded into an earlier Act?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. William Harris’s own sentences
This file agrees the deputation happened, who went, and what they asked, from the Australian
Dictionary of Biography and the 1928 photograph caption. Contemporary reports in The West
Australian and The Daily News of March 1928 should still be read word for word. Later articles quote
those papers in reported speech. This file does not turn that reported speech into a first-person
invention.
Question. Why might a later writer change “they claimed” into “I said,” and what is lost when that
happens?

4. Neville’s 1937 words, and later retellings
The typographic close line, and the sentences about taking children, are from the official 1937
conference report. They are often shortened later. Check the report itself, including the conference
resolution on “absorption,” before trusting a later one-line version.
Question. What does the full page do that a single famous sentence does not?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Moore River, with care
The Moore River Native Settlement (Mogumber) opened in 1918 under the 1905 Act. It is a place of
removal, family separation, and later testimony. This file names it because the 1928 deputation asked
for it to be closed. It does not invent a day in the settlement, and it does not print photographs of
children. If a class takes this further, it should do so with the relevant Aboriginal communities, and
with AIATSIS guidance.
Question. What can a law and a deputation show, and what can they not show, about a place like
Moore River?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Other Protection Acts
New South Wales had an Aborigines Protection Board from 1883 and an Aborigines Protection Act in
1909. Queensland’s 1897 Act is often treated as a model. This file’s sharp focus is Western Australia,
because the 1905 Act, Neville, Moore River, and the 1928 deputation can be held in one frame. The
other Acts still matter.
Question. If “protection” was a word used in more than one colony, what would you need in order
to answer the case question for the whole continent?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Premier Collier’s “great obligation”
Later accounts say Collier recognised “a great obligation to do justice to the Aboriginal, because [the
white man] had deprived him of his country.” That line should be checked against the March 1928
newspapers. The Act was not changed at that meeting.
Question. What is the difference between a recorded promise of consideration, and a change in the
law?

Teacher Note

PROTECTION · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE
DRAFT, PENDING CONSULTATION
Draft, pending consultation. This case asks whether “protection” ever meant protection, including for
Aboriginal people in Western Australia under the Aborigines Act 1905, and at the Moore River Native
Settlement. Teach it with the relevant Aboriginal communities — including Noongar communities,
and those connected with Moore River / Mogumber — and with AIATSIS guidance. Do not treat a
Year 10 finding as a substitute for that consultation.

Curriculum. Australian Curriculum: History v9, Year 10. AC9HH10K09: the causes of First Nations
Australians’ campaigns for rights and freedoms before 1965, such as discriminatory legislation and
policies, the 1938 Day of Mourning and the Stolen Generations. The 1928 deputation and the 1905
Act sit cleanly under that code. This is a Year 10 file. It is not written down to a younger year.

Quoted words, and framing

The typographic page is not a facsimile, and it is not a diary. It is a typographic setting of verified
wording from three dates. The opening line, “They called it protection.”, is this file’s frame. It is not
a historical quotation. The 1787 paragraph is from the Documenting a Democracy transcription of
Phillip’s Instructions, 25 April 1787. The 1905 lines are the long title of the Aborigines Act 1905
(WA), and section 8 as enacted in 1905, from the official statute text. The closing question is A. O.
Neville’s, from the official report of the Canberra conference of 21 to 23 April 1937. The handover
paragraph says, plainly, that these words were not spoken in one room.

Cultural safety

This file names the taking of children, because Neville said it, and because the 1905 Act made the
Chief Protector the legal guardian of children. It does not describe acts of violence in detail, it does
not print photographs of children, and it does not invent an Aboriginal child’s voice. Students
should not be asked to role-play a removal, or to write a first-person “Stolen Generations”
monologue. If a class is not ready for the 1937 sentences, stop at What is agreed and return later.
Offer students a way to step out. The language of the 1905 Act and of Neville’s 1937 speech is racist
in its official categories. It is reproduced here as evidence, clearly attributed, not as this book’s voice.

Conflicts and flags

The 1787 manuscript wording (“Savages” / “Natives”) is flagged in Super Sleuths. Section 8 as
reserved in 1905 is not identical with later reprints that include the 1911 mother-exclusion words;
this file keeps the dates apart. William Harris’s exact spoken sentences were not checked word for
word against The West Australian and The Daily News in this build, so they are not printed as
quotations on the student page; the deputation’s date, members, and asks follow the Australian

Great Sandy Island, early July 1836
We have been on this sand for nearly three weeks now. The longboat is useless. Six of the men took what
they could carry and walked south. They said they would find Moreton Bay. We have heard nothing.
The people of this island came soon after we landed. They stood off at first, watching. When they saw
we had little food left they came closer. One older man pointed at the pandanus and made the sign for
eating. We gave him a brass button. He brought fish.
Eliza is still with us. Her husband the Captain is weaker every day. The wound in his shoulder has not
closed. She sits beside him most of the hours and does not speak much. When the women of the island
come she turns her face away. They have tried to cover her arms and shoulders with a mixture of grease
and charcoal. She will not let them. She says it is filthy. They shrug and leave her in the sun.
Yesterday two of the men who stayed with us were taken away with a party of the island people. They
went quietly. I do not know if they were asked or ordered. Eliza watched them go and said nothing.
Later she told me, very low, that she believes we are prisoners. I asked her how she knew. She said, “They
took our clothes. They make us carry wood. What else would you call it?”
I said the men who left us on the beach took more than the island people have. She did not answer.
This morning the Captain could not stand. Eliza held his head while he drank a little water the island
women had brought in a shell. One of them stayed and watched. Eliza did not thank her.
I am writing this on the back of a chart page. If anyone finds it, know that we are alive, that the island
people have not killed us, and that Eliza Fraser believes we are captives. I am no longer certain what I
believe.
The light is going. The women are calling the children in. Eliza has not moved from her husband’s
side.

C. Brown

ELIZA FRASER · YEAR 9 · READ

Was Eliza Fraser a captive, or a guest?
The wreck of the Stirling Castle · K’gari, May–August 1836

Draft, pending consultation with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation.
Read the letter through to the last line. Then read what the 1836 file can agree on. After that, three
people who were there will be asked the same three questions.

CASE FILE: FRASER / STIRLING CASTLE
Date of incident
Location

Status

May–August 1836

A coral reef north of Moreton Bay → K’gari (then Great Sandy Island)

Unresolved contradictions

Key claims still disputed

– Was Captain James Fraser speared, or did he die of starvation or injury?
– Was Eliza Fraser a captive, or a guest who was kept alive?
– Did the Butchulla people save the survivors, or mistreat them?
– Which of Eliza’s later statements match the other survivors?

WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1836 FILE, AND AFTER
On the night of 21 May 1836 the brig Stirling Castle, James Fraser master, struck a coral reef well to
the north of Moreton Bay. (Later writers often say Swain Reefs. That identification is disputed, and
the wreck has not been found.) The survivors took to a longboat and a pinnace and headed south,
hoping to reach the convict settlement at Moreton Bay. Some later accounts say Eliza, who was
pregnant, gave birth in the leaking boat and that the baby lived only a short time. That claim is not in
her official narrative of 6 September 1836, and it is not treated here as settled.
The longboat was beached about twenty miles south of Sandy Cape, on the island Europeans called
Great Sandy Island and the Butchulla people call K’gari, around mid-June. Some of the crew walked
south toward Moreton Bay. Captain Fraser and the first mate, Charles Brown, both died after the
landing. A rescue party from Moreton Bay, guided by the convict John Graham, brought Eliza Fraser,
the second mate John Baxter, and other survivors out in mid-August. They had been on the island
and the nearby mainland for roughly six to eight weeks.
On 7 June 2023 the island’s official name was restored to K’gari.

Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber and other colours, used in Super Sleuths, mark what is
still disputed or was added later.

A NOTE ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE RECORDS
The 1836–37 records use the language of the period, including words that are offensive. They appear
only as short, attributed quotations, not as the language of this case file.

A published Butchulla reading of these weeks is essential to the case, but it is not an 1836 eyewitness
statement. The 1836 file never asked the people who lived on K’gari, and this case will not invent a
speaker to fill the gap. Those perspectives belong in Super Sleuths, under “Not asked.”

Eliza Fraser

Eliza Anne Fraser · captain’s wife, survivor

A formal statement taken at Moreton Bay after the rescue.
Source. “Mrs Fraser’s Narrative. The Brig ‘Stirling Castle’,” Moreton Bay, 6 September 1836. Colonial
Secretary’s papers (NSW), item 33054-002544, State Library of Queensland / FromThePage. Out of
copyright.

What they said. “We were now portioned off to different masters, who employed us in

carrying, Wood, water and bark, and treated us with the greatest cruelty.” At the close of
the same statement: “During the whole of my detention among the Natives I was treated
A silhouette, not a likeness.
with the greatest cruelty…” When her husband lay dying, “I was always prevented from
approaching him or rendering him any assistance.” Graham, she wrote, “spoke to the
Natives for some time and after a good deal of altercation succeeded in getting me away.”

Could they really have seen it? She was there after the landing, and she was there when

Graham came. She was not on the pinnace after it parted. She could not see what Butchulla
people intended. The 1836 statement already speaks of detention and masters. The London book
of 1838 goes much further.

Why might they say it? In 1836 she was a newly widowed woman giving a formal statement at
a penal settlement, already the subject of a subscription. In 1837, in London, she stood to gain
public sympathy and money, and, the Australian Dictionary of Biography records, presented
herself as a penniless widow after she had remarried and had already been assisted in Sydney.
Those facts do not prove the 1836 statement false. They are reasons to read each version in its
moment.

John Graham

John Graham · convict guide to the rescue party

A memorandum written to claim a reward, after the expedition.
Source. “Memorandum of the Real fact … of John Graham,” received 4 January 1837, Colonial Secretary’s
papers, item 33054-002543, SLQ / FromThePage. Supported by Fyans to the Colonial Secretary, 6
September 1836 (33054-002546), and by Lieutenant Otter’s letter, 27 August 1836 (33054-002547).

What they said. He writes that he “freed Mrs. Frazier from Seven hundred Canniballs

and savages” — the language of the penal colony, not a Butchulla account — but then
describes how: “getting the tribes that claimed him as there friend to stand by him while he
A silhouette, not a likeness.
claimed her as his or the (spirit of his wife) he succeeded to take her from than frightfull
place … and carried her upwards of 40 miles with the assistance of 4 blacks that came with
him from the mountains.” A note on the same memorandum explains “their belief of all
whites being spirits of their dead.” Fyans, who was not in the camp, added: “to him alone
are we indebted for the recovery of Mrs Frazer.”

Could they really have seen it? He had lived among Aboriginal people north of Moreton Bay
from 1827 to 1833 and, by his own and Otter’s account, could go into a camp unarmed. Otter
confirms that Graham came back “with four natives” and that Eliza was waiting close by for a
cloak. He was not a neutral observer.

Why might they say it? To obtain a remission or a reward, after “profferd Rewards and

Promises from Capt Fyans.” That interest is openly on the page. It does not cancel the detail
about a spirit-wife claim and Aboriginal assistance, which Otter independently places four
Aboriginal men at the handover.

What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________

Charles Otter

Lieutenant Charles Otter · 4th (King’s Own) Regiment

The official letter of the officer who led the rescue party.
Source. Letter to the Commandant, Moreton Bay, 27 August 1836, Colonial Secretary’s papers, item 33054002547, SLQ / FromThePage.

What they said. He first met two survivors on Bribie Island who, he says, “I at first took

to be natives as they were quite black and perfectly naked.” Of the later recovery: “Graham
appeared with four natives and gave us the satisfying intelligence that he had succeeded, &
A silhouette, not a likeness. that Mrs Fraser was waiting close at hand for a cloak to cover her, as she had been stripped
by the natives from the very first as well as the rest … many of whom had been very
unwilling to give her up.” Earlier in the same letter: “the natives who also brought the men

in had shown them more kindness then any other tribe.” Graham, he says, “was obliged not
only to go unarmed, but to strip himself perfectly naked when he went amongst them.”

Could they really have seen it? He saw the two men on Bribie, the handover on the sand,

and Eliza when she came to the party. He did not see the camp from which Graham brought her.
He waited at a prearranged mark in the sand. His phrase “in the hands of the natives” is his
official English. It sits in the same letter as “more kindness then any other tribe.”

Why might they say it? He was reporting to his commandant, recommending Graham, and

describing a “difficult and hazardous duty” the Governor later praised. He had reason to stress
danger and success. He also recorded kindness and Aboriginal assistance, which he did not have
to include.

WHY IT STILL MATTERS
Back in Sydney, then later in England, Eliza’s story was told and retold. Newspapers and
pamphlets described “savages,” captivity, and horrors. Money was raised for her. Books
appeared. The island came to be known as Fraser Island. Those sensational versions helped to
shape colonial ideas about Aboriginal people along the coast. They also sold. In 2023 the island’s
official name was restored to K’gari — a change the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation has
described as respect, after a name taken away through disrespect. The wreck itself is
straightforward. The weeks that followed, and what was later made of them, are not. That is why
the file is still open.

Teacher Note

ELIZA FRASER AND THE WRECK OF THE STIRLING CASTLE · YEAR 9
CONSULTATION REQUIRED
This case is a draft, pending consultation with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation, the RNTBC

for K’gari, and with the families or Elders the Corporation names. It is not a finished student file.
Follow the AIATSIS Code of Ethics and the AIATSIS guidelines for ethical publishing. No sacred
or secret material. No invented Butchulla speaker, character, or likeness. Teacher preview
required.

Curriculum link: Australian Curriculum: History v9, Year 9

AC9HH9K03: the causes and effects of European contact and extension of settlement,
including their impact on the First Nations Peoples of Australia. AC9HH9K06: different

experiences and perspectives of colonisers, settlers and First Nations Australians and the
impact of these experiences on changes to Australian society’s ideas, beliefs and values. Also
useful: skills AC9HH9S06 (compare perspectives in sources) and AC9HH9S07 (analyse
different and contested historical interpretations).

What’s true about the opener · the letter from Charles Brown

This note is for teachers. It is not printed on the letter’s student page, which is written to look
authentic. The page is not labelled invented, because the book’s standing rule is that what’s
true sits only here.
The letter is not a historical document. No letter from Charles Brown on Great Sandy Island is
known. He was real: the first mate (Eliza’s narrative; Baxter’s “Chief mate”; later scholarship).

Dramatic irony, not for the student page. Eliza’s official narrative says that after Captain

Fraser’s death she and Brown were put across to the mainland in a canoe; Brown, already terribly
injured (she describes burns with firebrands, and that “the flesh had fallen from his feet”), died
three or four days after the crossing. She says she was prevented from taking him food. The letter’s
line “know that we are alive, that the island people have not killed us” is written in a voice that does
not know that. Students should meet the letter first. Teachers may return to Brown’s death after the
witnesses, if they judge the class ready; it needs a content note.

Constructed scenes and details that were kept, because they carry the approved voice and are

not clearly contradicted, but are not in the 1836 statements: the brass button and the pandanus sign
(Eliza says fish were obtained in exchange for “articles of wearing apparel”); the grease and charcoal
on Eliza’s arms (a later interpretive reading of practical care, not a detail in the official file); the shell
of water; “two of the men who stayed with us were taken away” as a single witnessed scene; Brown’s
spoken uncertainty on the sand; the “back of a chart page.”

pages.alt: Page 58. Eliza Fraser. The shoulder wound. The letter says “The wound in his shoulder has not closed.” It does not say he arrived on the island already wounded. Eliza attributes the wound to a spear, “a little below the
pages.text:
The shoulder wound. The letter says “The wound in his shoulder has not closed.” It does not say
he arrived on the island already wounded. Eliza attributes the wound to a spear, “a little below the
blade bone,” after they were already in a camp and he had been unable, through debility, to carry a

large log of wood. “Of this wound he never recovered,” and he died eight or nine days afterwards. In
an early-July letter, a wound that “has not closed” can fit a spearing earlier in the stay. Teachers
should not let students assume it was a wreck or boat injury.

Two wording changes only in the approved text. Everything else of the approved letter was kept.
1. The date line. “Late July 1836” became “early July 1836.” Eliza’s narrative of 6 September 1836
says they beached about twenty miles south of Sandy Cape “about three weeks since our departure

from the wreck” (the wreck was the night of 21 May, so around mid-June). Barbara Dawson, In the
Eye of the Beholder (ANU Press, 2014), gives about 12 June. The letter also says “We have been on
this sand for nearly three weeks now.” Early July keeps that sentence consistent with a mid-June
landing.

2. First contact. “The people of this island came on the third day” became “The people of this island
came soon after we landed.” Eliza’s official narrative: “Directly we landed the Natives came down in
crowds.” “They stood off at first, watching” was kept, as a constructed detail of cautious approach,
not as a delay of two days.

Other details flagged, not changed. “Six of the men… walked south.” Eliza does not give a

number. Dawson (2014) reconstructs six men walking south; three reached Moreton Bay. The
number six is a later reconstruction, not a figure in the 1836 statements. It was kept, with this flag,
because it is the scholarly number and is not clearly false.

What’s true? The case

Eliza Fraser, John Graham and Charles Otter were all real. The short summaries use their own
writing. Words in quotation marks come from Eliza’s narrative of 6 September 1836, Graham’s
memorandum received 4 January 1837, and Otter’s letter of 27 August 1836. The three images
are plain period-style silhouettes with name cards, not likenesses of the people named. No
period portrait from life has been invented for this file.
An optional Super Sleuths extension follows My finding, and is on the website at
robmac10.github.io/eliza-fraser-case/#sleuth. It reopens colour marking, reliability labels, the full
1836 witness files, published Butchulla perspectives under “Not asked,” and a more rigorous finding.
The Three Laws are cited from the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation’s “People & Country” page
(bac-kgari.org/people-and-country) and marked for consultation. They are not evidence of what any
named person said in 1836, and are not to be printed as a finished student extract until the
Corporation has been consulted.

Uncertainties · still open

The baby in the boat. In the ADB and some later histories; not in the 6 September 1836 official
narrative. Leave unsettled.

Bracewell and Russell. Still to be checked: locate the primary text of David Bracewell’s 1842
claim and Henry Stuart Russell’s version before citing them. Official 1836–37 records name
Graham, not Bracewell.

Where exactly the ship struck. A reef north of Moreton Bay, 21 May 1836, is agreed. Swain

Reefs is a common later identification, disputed by Geraghty (2021) in favour of Frederick Reef. The
wreck has not been found.

Dates of the recovery. Graham’s memorandum disagrees with itself. Otter’s letter is dated 27
August. The ADB gives the party’s return to Brisbane as 21 August 1836.

Names and spellings. Corralis / Corallas / Corrales / Carrallis; Youlden / Youldrow / Gouldron;
Dayman / Daymens; Darge / Dargo / Large. This draft uses one form on the student page and
records the variants here.

The 1837 London wording. A sentence often repeated, that the Lord Mayor had “never heard

anything so truly dreadful,” is cited by Iain McCalman from contemporary papers; verify against the
newspaper before quoting it in the finished case. It is not quoted here.

Butchulla wording in the finished case. Quote only page-exact, cleared extracts. The Three
Laws are cited from the Corporation’s website and marked for consultation.

Afterlives of the story. Modern Butchulla and scholarly readings (Foley, Behrendt, and others)

argue that the captivity-and-cannibal story fed a colonial picture of Aboriginal people and helped to
justify dispossession, including the name “Fraser Island.” That is an interpretation about afterlives,
not a finding the 1836 file can settle on its own.

Cultural safety · reminder
Consultation first, with the Butchulla Aboriginal Corporation and those it names. Use K’gari for the
island, and “Fraser Island” only when discussing the colonial renaming and its undoing. Use
Butchulla as the Corporation does (sources also spell Badtjala, Badjala, Butchalla). Do not collapse
Butchulla with neighbouring groups. Period words such as “savages” and “cannibals” may appear
only as short, clearly attributed quotations, with a content note. They are not the book’s language.
Avoid sensationalism, including the sexual-fear tropes of the captivity genre; if later sources raise
them, they belong in this teacher note, not in the opener.

The stockade is quiet. I keep thinking about the

Camp, on the other side of Ballarat. I wonder if
anyone is asleep there at all.
Our tent, Eureka

Sunday, 3 December. Before dawn.

Something woke me. A sound? Da was snoring. Ma
was asleep with the baby. Outside, the sky was

turning from black to the dark grey just before
dawn.

Then I heard it again. Feet. Lots of feet. Moving
together. And the soft jingle of harness, as if
horses were being walked very slowly.

I crept to the tent flap and lifted the corner.

Out in the grey half-light, beyond the stockade, a
long line of shapes was spreading out. They were
moving forward. Quietly. Steadily. Closer.

I opened my mouth to call Da. Someone somewhere
shouted a warning.

CRACK! A shot split the dark.

Was it from the stockade? From the soldiers? From
somewhere off in the bush? In the grey light, with
the echo bouncing around the gully, I could not
tell. And then I—

EUREKA STOCKADE · YEAR 5 · THE CASE

Who fired first?

Eureka Stockade, Ballarat, 3 December 1854
Before dawn on Sunday 3 December 1854, soldiers and police marched from the Government Camp at
Ballarat to a stockade built by gold diggers on the Eureka lead. Captain Thomas led 276 men. Inside the
stockade there were far fewer diggers. Shooting broke out. Within minutes it was over. Everyone agrees
there was shooting. Not everyone agrees who started it.
Nell’s Diary stops at the first shot. These three people were there. Each left a real record. Ask each one:
What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · Why might they say it?

Peter Lalor

The diggers’ leader. Inside the stockade.

Lalor was inside the stockade when the shooting began. About four months later he wrote
to the newspapers: “I believe that one or two signal shots were fired by our sentries.” He
also wrote: “The military fired the first volley.” A signal shot is a warning. A volley is many
guns fired together. Notice the words “I believe”: he is not sure about the sentry shots.
Source: Peter Lalor, “To the Colonists of Victoria”, Geelong Advertiser, 9 April 1855, and The Argus, 10 April
1855, p. 7.
Peter Lalor, 1856

What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________

Captain John Wellesley Thomas
Commander of the soldiers and police.

Thomas led the soldiers and police to the stockade. In his report, written that same day, he
said his men “were received by rather sharp and well-directed fire from the insurgents,
without word or challenge on their part; then, and not till then, I ordered the bugle to sound
the ‘commence firing;’” (“Insurgents” means rebels.) His report does not mention a warning
shot from a sentry.
Source: Captain J. W. Thomas’s report to Head Quarters, Camp, Ballaarat, 3 December 1854.

later in life

Raffaello Carboni

An Italian digger. Asleep in a tent beside the stockade.

Carboni was asleep in his tent, which he said was “the second from the stockade, on the hill,
west.” He wrote: “I awoke. Sunday morning. It was full dawn, not daylight. A discharge of
musketry—then a round from the bugle—the command ‘forward’.” He heard firing first,
then the bugle. He does not say which side fired that first discharge.
Source: Raffaello Carboni, The Eureka Stockade (Melbourne, 1855), Chapter LVI.

Teacher Note

Curriculum link: Australian Curriculum: HASS v9, Year 5
(History)

AC9HS5K03: “the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations

Australians and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an
Australian colony”. A listed elaboration names “the impact of the Eureka Stockade on the
development of democracy”, and another poses “What if Peter Lalor had encouraged gold
miners to pay rather than resist licence fees?”

Skills: AC9HS5S02, “to locate, collect and organise information and data from primary
and secondary sources in a range of formats”; AC9HS5S04, “to evaluate primary and
secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives”. Also supports
AC9HS5S01 (developing questions) and the civics description AC9HS5K07 (citizens
working together towards a civic goal).

What’s true? Nell’s Diary

This note is for teachers. It is not printed in the student-facing diary, which is written to
look authentic.

Who is made up? Nell, her father, mother and the baby are invented, as are the trooper

at the licence hunt, Nell borrowing an onion, everything the Byrnes say and do, her classwork headings, the place lines at the head of each entry, and Mrs Hayes’s margin notes,
hint notes, spelling corrections and words to Nell. The Byrnes are Irish, like many families
near the Eureka lead. Chinese diggers worked the Ballarat goldfield and paid licence fees,
but no particular Chinese person here is named or invented.

Who is real? Peter Lalor, Captain John Wellesley Thomas, Raffaello Carboni, Anastasia

Hayes and Timothy Hayes were all real. Their actions come from the case-file sources.
Lalor’s words on the stump are retold, not quoted; the oath, kneeling and “Amen” come
from Carboni’s 1855 book. Later notices say she pushed through the soldiers to reach her
chained husband and told his guards what she thought of them, but her exact words are not
certain. A later tradition credits Anastasia Hayes with helping to sew the Southern Cross
flag. That claim is disputed. She is also said to have nursed the wounded.

The school and the sketch Mrs Hayes taught at the Roman Catholic school Dean

Matthew Downing opened on 1 April 1853 in the slab-and-canvas St Alipius chapel, Ballarat
East (now St Alipius Parish School, Victoria Street). The image on the diary is Eugene von
Guérard’s January 1854 sketch Catholic Chapel on the Gravel Pit Line, Ballarat, State
Library of Victoria, accession H12532 (this work is out of copyright; no copyright
restrictions apply): https://viewer.slv.vic.gov.au/?entity=IE1446748 The spelling is Alipius.

Sources: https://saballarat.catholic.edu.au/st-alipius-history.html and
https://eurekapedia.org/Anastasia_Hayes.

What really happened? From the records: the licence hunts; licences burnt on Bakery

Hill on 29 November; stone-throwing on 30 November; the oath under the flag; the slab
stockade; the notice about lights; Carboni frying steak and noting the empty stockade on
Saturday; and the soldiers’ silent march before dawn on 3 December. From her tent, Nell
could not have known the soldiers’ numbers or their time of march. She only saw what she
could see, in the dark.

What isn’t certain? Witnesses disagree on the time of the attack. Nobody knows exactly
how many died: diggers, soldiers, and at least one woman. People still argue about who
sewed the flag (women of the goldfields, or tent makers or men using tent cloth) and who
fired first.

What happened next? The stockade was taken in minutes. Lalor was badly wounded

and hidden by friends. Thirteen men, including Timothy Hayes and Raffaello Carboni, were
tried for high treason in 1855 and found not guilty. The licence was soon replaced, and
Lalor was later elected to Victoria’s parliament.
Students may trust the diary as real. Reveal that Nell is invented and ask how they could
have checked.
An easy-read version in plain hand-print is available online (Easy-read switch) for
students who find the joined hand hard to read.

summaries use their own writing. Words in quotation marks come from Lalor’s 1855 letter,
Thomas’s report of 3 December 1854, and Carboni’s book of 1855. Nothing on the witness
page is a reconstruction.

In front of a banner, Young, New South Wales

Painted 1861 · Still here

The banner is still here.
Someone painted it on a tent flap in 1861. ROLL UP. NO CHINESE. A
cross, and stars, and those words, big enough to carry at the
front of a march. And then someone kept it. And then a museum put
it behind glass, as if it were only an object.
I stood in front of it and tried to imagine two or three thousand
people walking behind that cloth, toward camps of men who had
come here to dig. I tried to imagine the petitions that came
after, written in English and in Chinese, asking to be paid for
what was taken and smashed. I tried to imagine the courtroom
where almost everyone walked free.

The banner survived. I’m not sure the people it was
aimed at were meant to. Who started it, and did anyone
pay? The file is still open. The cloth is still here.

THE LAMBING FLAT RIOTS, 1860–61 · YEAR 9 · READ

The Lambing Flat riots, 1860–61
Who started it, and did anyone pay?

What is agreed

Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was
added later.

The Lambing Flat riots were a series of anti-Chinese attacks on the Burrangong goldfield, New
South Wales, between November 1860 and July 1861. Lambing Flat was one part of the field.
The main settlement later became the town of Young. The Riot Act was read on 27 January and
on 14 July 1861.

The first anti-Chinese riot on this field is dated 13 November 1860. Further attacks followed,
including 8–9 December 1860, 27 January 1861, and 19 February 1861. On 8–9 December,

reports of two Chinese deaths were investigated by Superintendent Henry Zouch of the Mounted
Police, who found that no deaths had occurred and that the reports had come from European
miners.

The worst attack was on 30 June 1861. A crowd of European, American and Australasian-born
miners, commonly put at 2,000 to 3,000, marched with a band and the “Roll Up – No Chinese”
banner from Allandale (Tipperary Gully) to camps at Sawpit Gully and then Back Creek.
Numbers of Chinese people at those camps are not agreed in the sources: one careful local
account gives about 200–600 at Sawpit Gully and 400–1,000 at Back Creek; other accounts
give different figures. Chinese petitioners later said they were beaten, that property was
destroyed, and that one of them, Tom Me, had his hair cut off. One later synthesis says about
200 Chinese people were wounded, and that no one was killed on 30 June. This file records
those claims, and does not invent a death toll the record has not settled.

The banner, painted on a tent flap, is now held at the Young Historical Museum. It shows a

Police arrested men identified as leaders. On the night of 14 July 1861 a crowd attacked the
police camp; the police broke it up with gunfire and a mounted charge. One rioter, William
Lupton, was killed. Troops, sailors and police reinforcements later arrived from Sydney and
remained for a time. Premier Charles Cowper had already visited Burrangong in early March
1861, between the earlier riots and the June attack.

Most men tried for the riots were acquitted. Two were convicted: Claremont Owen, a
watchmaker, sentenced to two years’ hard labour in Darlinghurst Gaol for his part in the 14 July
riot; and William Spicer, a miner, sentenced to two years’ imprisonment for his part in the 30
June riot. Spicer was released on the Queen’s Birthday in 1862 after a petition of 2,989
signatures from the Lachlan goldfield. Some later retellings say only Spicer was convicted. This
file follows the court record that both Owen and Spicer were sentenced.

Chinese miners and storekeepers petitioned the New South Wales government for
compensation, in English and in Chinese. William Campbell, as a commissioner, examined
claims. For losses on 30 June 1861 he reported 1,568 claimants asking a total of £40,623, and
recommended that £4,240 be paid to 706 people. In September 1863 lists of approved claims
were published in the NSW Government Gazette. In March 1864, 94 Chinese signatories at
Tuena petitioned that their approved claims had still not been paid, almost three years after the
riot. Whether the full amount recommended was ever paid remains an open question in the
sources.

Later in 1861 the New South Wales Parliament passed the Chinese Immigrants Regulation and

Restriction Act 1861 (often called the Chinese Immigration Restriction Act), which imposed a
£10 tax on Chinese immigrants arriving by ship. The Gold Fields Act 1861 also allowed the
restriction of “aliens” on the fields. Those laws sit in the same year as the riots. This file does not
pretend the Parliament had only one reason for passing them.
